# Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → newest | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. Newest days lag about 5 days and are revised. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | Added because modeled gusts run low. Confirmed in Step 2 |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

# Design & architecture

> Draft. Filled in as each step lands, and finalized in Step 9.

## System architecture
See the diagram in [plan.md](plan.md#architecture-target). Components:

| Component | Where | Talks to |
|---|---|---|
| Chat UI + widgets | `src/app/` (Next.js App Router) | Only our own API routes |
| API routes | `src/app/api/` | `src/core` |
| Auth proxy | `src/proxy.ts` | Guards pages + API (Basic Auth); cron uses `CRON_SECRET` |
| Agent | `src/core/agent/` | OpenRouter (LLM), tools |
| Tools | `src/core/tools/` | Repositories + scoring/stats |
| Scoring & stats | `src/core/scoring/`, `src/core/stats/` | Nothing: pure functions |
| Ingest | `src/core/ingest/` | Open-Meteo, FEMA NRI, Supabase |
| Repositories | `src/core/db/` | Supabase Postgres |

## Repository structure
```
src/app/         Next.js only (pages, API routes, components)
src/core/        framework-free logic (lint-enforced): config, domain, errors, db, …
scripts/         CLI entry points (db:check, session:export; later ingest, eval)
supabase/        SQL migrations (schema + hub seed)
docs/            plan, decisions, assumptions, design, session log
```

## Data storage choice
**Supabase Postgres**, because:
- The data is relational and small (36 hubs × ~2,200 days ≈ 80k weather rows).
- SQL makes the evals' "expected values" and ad-hoc analysis easy.
- It's hosted and free, and pairs well with Vercel.
- Built-in RLS lets us lock the tables down completely (server-only access).
- One store holds the hubs, the cached weather and FEMA data, score history, chat memory and the event log.
  No extra services.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet

A weather risk intelligence agent for a logistics company's US distribution hubs.
Analysts chat with it to find out which hubs are most exposed to severe weather, compare hubs,
and understand *why* a hub is risky, to help decide where to invest in resilience upgrades.

> 🚧 Work in progress. Built step by step. See [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md).

## Docs
- [Plan](docs/plan.md): architecture, tables, steps
- [Decision log](docs/decisions.md): every choice and why
- [Assumptions, uncertainty & scope](docs/assumptions.md)
- [Design](docs/design.md)
- [AI session log](docs/session/): the full conversation with the coding agent

## Run locally
Requirements: Node 22+, a Supabase project.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local     # then fill in the values (see comments in the file)
npm run db:check               # verifies the database connection: lists the hubs
npm run dev                    # http://localhost:3000
```

## Scripts
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` | Start the app locally |
| `npm test` | Unit tests (Vitest) |
| `npm run typecheck` | TypeScript check |
| `npm run lint` | ESLint (includes the rule keeping `src/core` free of Next.js) |
| `npm run db:check` | Connect to Supabase and list hubs per region |
| `npm run session:export -- <file.jsonl>` | Export the AI session log to `docs/session/` (scrubbed) |

## Database
SQL migrations live in [supabase/migrations/](supabase/migrations/). Apply them in order to a fresh
Supabase project (SQL editor or Supabase CLI). The second migration seeds the 36 hubs.

## Data attribution
Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Hazard data: FEMA National Risk Index.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet — Plan

Agreed on 2026-11-25 after a structured "grilling" session (see `docs/session/`).
Every individual choice and its reason is in [decisions.md](decisions.md).

## Goal
A chat agent that helps logistics analysts decide which distribution hubs are most
exposed to severe weather and should get resilience investment. It ranks, compares
and explains hubs using **deterministic, tested scoring code**. The LLM only chooses
tools and explains their results. It never invents numbers.

## Architecture (target)
```
Browser (Next.js UI: Roboto, dark glass)
  │  POST /api/chat {sessionId, message}  → streams progress + text + validated answer
  │  GET  /api/widgets                    → top hubs, hazard leaders, data status
  ▼
proxy.ts — Basic Auth on everything except /api/cron/* (uses CRON_SECRET)
  ▼
src/app/api/*  (thin: Zod-parse → call core → format response/errors)
  ▼
src/core/  (no Next.js; testable alone)
  agent/   AI SDK v7 streamText + 4 tools + Output.object(answer schema)
           → validate → code overrides confidence/disclaimer → retry once → error
  tools/   rank_hubs · compare_hubs · get_weather_stat · explain_hub_score
  scoring/ pure: thresholds → per-hazard 0–100 → overall → level → confidence
  stats/   pure: counts / % / ranges over daily rows
  ingest/  incremental: Open-Meteo + FEMA → DB → scoring → nightly snapshot
  db/      Supabase repositories (server-only secret key)
  ▼                    ▼                          ▼
Supabase Postgres   OpenRouter (LLM + Jev)   Open-Meteo archive · FEMA NRI ArcGIS
        ▲
Vercel Cron (daily) → /api/cron/ingest      npm run ingest (first full load, local)
```

## Database tables
Every table has `created_at` + `updated_at` (trigger-maintained). RLS on, no public policies.

| Table | Holds |
|---|---|
| `hubs` | id slug, name, state, Census region, lat/lon, timezone, county FIPS/name, active |
| `weather_daily` | hub × date: snowfall, min temp, precipitation, max gust, max apparent temp |
| `fema_nri` | per hub: NRI version + annualized frequency per hazard + raw record |
| `score_snapshots` | per hub per ingest run: overall, level, top hazard, breakdown, confidence, window, scoring_version |
| `chat_sessions`, `chat_messages` | server-side conversation memory incl. tool results |
| `events` | append-only log (ingest, scoring, validation failures, retries, guard decisions, errors), grouped by `correlation_id` |

## Scoring (summary)
- 6 hazards and weights: hurricane 25%, winter 20%, flood/rain 20%, severe storms (tornado + hail) 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%.
- Each hazard is scored 0–100 on a fixed absolute scale. Mixed hazards are 50% observed (Open-Meteo) + 50% FEMA annualized frequency.
- Overall = 60% weighted average + 40% highest hazard. Levels: Low 0–33, Medium 34–66, High 67–100.
- Confidence (High/Medium/Low) is computed in code from data completeness and the number of sources.
- Rolling 5-year window ending at the newest available day. The relative rank among hubs is shown next to the score.

## Steps (one branch + PR each; Yarden merges)
| # | Step | New env vars |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Supabase project, scaffold, lint boundary, Vitest, env validation, error helper, schema + events, 36-hub seed, docs, session export | `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` |
| 2 | Open-Meteo + FEMA clients, incremental paced ingest, first full load, check wind-gust distribution | — |
| 3 | Anchor values reviewed with real data → scoring test-first → snapshots | — |
| 4 | Agent: tools, answer schema + validation + retry, recommendation rules, chat history | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_MODEL` |
| 5 | Streaming `POST /api/chat`, `/api/widgets`, cron route, Basic Auth | `APP_USERNAME`, `APP_PASSWORD`, `CRON_SECRET` |
| 6 | UI: chat, 3 widgets, per-answer charts | — |
| 7 | Eval set (13 cases) + `npm run eval` (`--url` for deployed) | — |
| 8 | Model bakeoff (3–4 models: accuracy → cost → speed), lock in the winner | — |
| 9 | README, design doc, final assumptions | — |
| 10 | Deploy to Vercel, env vars, cron, run evals against live URL | (same, in Vercel) |
| 11 | Phase 1.5: Jev guard (`typesafe/jev-1.14`, cutoff 0.4, 2 s fail-open, last 2 turns) + guard evals + cutoff tuning | `JEV_MODEL` |

## Later (order to be chosen)
Themed login page · dust storm hazard (NOAA Storm Events) · US map widget · abuse/off-topic
hardening · score-change alerts · 7-day forecast + NWS active alerts · per-hub local
thresholds · hub volume weighting · voice.

## Eval cases (Step 7)
1. Midwest winter ranking. 2. Miami vs Houston hurricane + flood. 3. Denver % snow days 2025.
4. "Why is Dallas high?" premise check. 5. False premise (Seattle hurricane). 6. Follow-up "why that one?".
7. Overall top 5. 8. Unknown city (Boise). 9. Dust storm (not scored). 10. Decision question.
11. Off-topic. 12. "Last year" = 2025. 13. Confidence matches code.

# Decision log

Every choice we made, and why, in plain language. Newest at the bottom of each section.
"Q#" refers to the question number in the planning session (`docs/session/`).

## Product & scope

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Name: **The Daily Prophet**. Original design, no Harry Potter logos, fonts, crests or characters. | Fun theme without copying anyone's brand. |
| D2 | **36 hubs**, one per major US metro, stored as rows in the database. Adding a city = adding a row. | The brief asked for 25–50 metros and for hubs to be data, not code. |
| D3 | "Midwest", "South" and so on use the **official US Census regions**. | Gives "Which Midwest hubs…" a clear, quotable definition. |
| D4 | A hub's location is the **city-center point**. FEMA data comes from the county that point is in. | Simple and consistent. A real warehouse can sit elsewhere in the metro (written down as an assumption). |
| D5 | **6 hazards**: winter (snow, cold, ice), flood/heavy rain, high wind, extreme heat, hurricane, severe storms (tornado + **hail**). (Q6) | Hail is one of the costliest hazards for trucks and roofs. Folding it into "severe storms" keeps 6 hazards and the same weights. |
| D6 | **Dust storms: not in Phase 1.** Added as the first feature after deploy, using NOAA Storm Events. (Q5, Q27) | We checked: it *is* possible, but it only matters for about 3 hubs and would add a data source to the critical path. Until then the agent says "not scored yet". |
| D7 | "Last year" = **calendar year 2025** by default. The agent says which period it used and offers the other one ("last 12 months"). (Q11) | Avoids ambiguity. Shows its work. |
| D8 | Answers to "should we invest in X?" carry a **recommendation**, and **code** adds a fixed disclaimer: weather exposure only, the final call belongs to the team. (Q23) | Analysts want a decision aid, but no one should trust an LLM 100%. |

## Data

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D9 | **Open-Meteo historical archive** for snow, cold, rain, wind and heat. **FEMA National Risk Index v1.20** (public ArcGIS service, no key) for hurricane, tornado, hail, flood, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, strong wind and heat wave. | Both are free public APIs. FEMA covers the rare-event hazards that 5 years of daily weather can't measure well. |
| D10 | Use FEMA **wherever it has the hazard**, not just for 4 hazards. (Q7) | Two sources per hazard is sturdier. The modeled weather data smooths out wind gusts, so FEMA balances that. "How many sources" then means something for confidence. |
| D11 | From FEMA, use **annualized frequency** (events per year), not FEMA's "risk score". (Q8) | FEMA's risk score ranks counties against each other and mixes in population and building value. Frequency is absolute and closest to "how often does this shut a hub down". |
| D12 | FEMA renamed riverine flood **RFLD → IFLD (Inland Flooding)**. Flood uses IFLD + CFLD (coastal). | Found while researching v1.20. |
| D13 | Data is fetched by an **ingest job**, not while a user chats. Tools only read the database. (Q11) | Fast, repeatable answers. Evals stay stable. External outages don't break chat. |
| D14 | Store **daily rows** from 2021-01-01 up to the newest available day. A **nightly cron** adds new days and re-fetches the last 7 (Open-Meteo revises them, about a 5-day lag). The first full load runs locally, paced. (Q11) | Open-Meteo counts 5 years for one city as about 130 calls, and Vercel's shared IPs hit limits sooner. Most nights the cron only fetches a few days. |
| D15 | Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest day. A snapshot is saved each night. (Q11) | Your idea. It makes "alert when a score changes" meaningful, and every season still counts 5 times. |

## Scoring

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D16 | Scores are **deterministic TypeScript**, written test-first. The LLM never invents numbers. (Q25) | Assignment requirement. It also makes answers checkable. |
| D17 | **Absolute** fixed scales per hazard, not scores relative to other hubs. The **relative rank** is shown next to the score ("Winter 41/100 · #12 of 36"). (Q28) | Relative scores would shift when a city is added and would always label someone "High". The local-vulnerability concern (5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta) is a later improvement: per-hub local thresholds. |
| D18 | Mixed hazards = **50% observed + 50% FEMA**, with sub-signals averaged within each half. FEMA "not applicable" counts as 0 with full confidence. (Q21) | Simple, explainable, symmetric. |
| D19 | Weights: hurricane 25%, winter 20%, flood 20%, severe storms 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%. Overall = 60% weighted average + 40% worst hazard. Levels Low 0–33 / Medium 34–66 / High 67–100. | Weighted by business impact. The "worst hazard" term keeps one severe hazard (Miami hurricanes) from being averaged away. |
| D20 | Thresholds: snow day ≥1 cm, heavy snow ≥15 cm, extreme cold min ≤−18 °C, heavy rain ≥50 mm, high wind gust ≥93 km/h **plus an advisory tier ≥72 km/h**, extreme heat apparent max ≥40 °C. One national value each. (Q28) | Checked against NWS criteria (links in assumptions.md). The extra wind tier exists because modeled data under-reports peak gusts. To be confirmed with real data in Step 2. |
| D21 | **Confidence is computed by code** from data completeness and the number of sources. The LLM's value is overridden. The same goes for hubs mentioned and data used: they must match the tool results. (Q14) | Confidence is a number-like claim, so the LLM must not invent it either. |
| D22 | Every snapshot stores a **`scoring_version`**. | So that "we changed the formula" never looks like "Dallas got riskier" (no false alerts). |

## Agent & API

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D23 | 4 tools: `rank_hubs`, `compare_hubs`, `get_weather_stat`, `explain_hub_score`. The hub list goes in the system prompt. (Q22) | Maps one-to-one to the question types in the brief. |
| D24 | Final answer is a **Zod-validated JSON** object: answer, outOfScope, hubsMentioned, dataUsed, premiseCheck, confidence, assumptions, limitations, followUpSuggestions, recommendation. Invalid → retry once → clear error. (Q23) | Assignment requirement: structured output between the LLM and our code. |
| D25 | **Conversation memory is stored on the server** (Supabase) by `sessionId`, including tool results. (Q12) | Follow-ups like "why that one?" reuse exact numbers. The client can't tamper with history. Gives an audit trail. |
| D26 | **Streaming**: progress lines and answer text stream live. The data panel appears only after the final JSON passes validation. (Q13) | Better UX (your call) without giving up validation. |
| D27 | LLM via **OpenRouter**, model in `OPENROUTER_MODEL`. Start with a strong model, then **pick the final one by a bakeoff on our eval set** (accuracy → cost → speed) before deploy. (Q15) | You can't choose the "right model" fairly without a measurement. |
| D28 | **Vercel AI SDK v7** (current major). | Supports tools and a validated structured output in one streaming call. |

## Safety & access

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D29 | **Username + password** on the whole site and API (Basic Auth now, themed login page later). $20 credit cap on the OpenRouter key. Message-length and agent-step limits. (Q16) | Stops strangers spending the LLM budget. Simplest thing that works first. |
| D30 | Out-of-scope guard: **Jev (`typesafe/jev-1.14`) via OpenRouter**, pinned version. Decline below **0.4** probability of being in scope. Give up after 2 s and let the question through. Jev sees the last 2 turns. Every decision is logged. (Q19, Q20, Q26) | 0.4 is a middle ground. Too high a cutoff refuses real follow-ups like "why?". The final cutoff will be tuned on eval data. More abuse protection is planned later. |

## Engineering

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D31 | **One Next.js app** with `src/core/` free of Next.js and React, **enforced by an ESLint rule**. (Q1) | Core logic can be tested and run from scripts and evals without the web framework. Simpler than a monorepo. |
| D32 | Supabase project **`daily-prophet` in us-east-1**, close to Vercel's default region. (Q2) | Low latency between the app and the DB. |
| D33 | **RLS on every table with no policies.** Only the server (secret key) can read or write. The browser never talks to the DB. | Nothing is exposed even if the public key leaks. |
| D34 | **Every table has `created_at` + `updated_at`** (a trigger keeps `updated_at` current), plus an **`events`** table that replaces a separate `ingest_runs` table. | Your standing rule: be able to track and analyze everything. One events table covers runs, failures, retries and guard decisions. |
| D35 | Errors at boundaries use **`ErrorName \|\| message \|\| function \|\| emoji`**, with a fixed emoji per boundary: 🦉 LLM, 🐸 Open-Meteo, 🦡 FEMA, 🐘 database, 🦄 API route, 🐍 Jev, 🦔 config. Users only see a clean `{error:{code,message}}`. (Q17) | Your format. A fixed emoji makes logs searchable by origin. |
| D36 | Hub IDs are **readable slugs** (`kansas-city`), not airport codes. | Clearer for the LLM, logs and humans. |
| D37 | **Tailwind CSS** for styling (it ships with the Next.js starter). | Fast to build the glass UI, and no extra dependency. |
| D38 | The hub seed is a **SQL migration**. Migrations are applied through the Supabase connection and also saved in `supabase/migrations/`. | The database can be rebuilt from the repo. |
| D39 | `@types/node` bumped to **v22** to match Node 22 (Vitest 5 requires it). | Fixes the install conflict. Matches the runtime. |
| D40 | **PR per step.** Claude opens it, Yarden reviews and merges. Claude never pushes to `main` (except the single empty initial commit an empty repo needs as a PR base). (Q3) | Review before anything lands. |
| D41 | The session log is exported to `docs/session/` with **private details scrubbed** (emails, keys, home path, login codes). The model's private reasoning blocks and internal bookkeeping records are left out. (Q4) | The assignment requires the full session, and the repo is public. |

# Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → newest | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. Newest days lag about 5 days and are revised. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | Added because modeled gusts run low. Confirmed in Step 2 |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

# Design & architecture

> Draft. Filled in as each step lands, and finalized in Step 9.

## System architecture
See the diagram in [plan.md](plan.md#architecture-target). Components:

| Component | Where | Talks to |
|---|---|---|
| Chat UI + widgets | `src/app/` (Next.js App Router) | Only our own API routes |
| API routes | `src/app/api/` | `src/core` |
| Auth proxy | `src/proxy.ts` | Guards pages + API (Basic Auth); cron uses `CRON_SECRET` |
| Agent | `src/core/agent/` | OpenRouter (LLM), tools |
| Tools | `src/core/tools/` | Repositories + scoring/stats |
| Scoring & stats | `src/core/scoring/`, `src/core/stats/` | Nothing: pure functions |
| Ingest | `src/core/ingest/` | Open-Meteo, FEMA NRI, Supabase |
| Repositories | `src/core/db/` | Supabase Postgres |

## Repository structure
```
src/app/         Next.js only (pages, API routes, components)
src/core/        framework-free logic (lint-enforced): config, domain, errors, db, …
scripts/         CLI entry points (db:check, session:export; later ingest, eval)
supabase/        SQL migrations (schema + hub seed)
docs/            plan, decisions, assumptions, design, session log
```

## Data storage choice
**Supabase Postgres**, because:
- The data is relational and small (36 hubs × ~2,200 days ≈ 80k weather rows).
- SQL makes the evals' "expected values" and ad-hoc analysis easy.
- It's hosted and free, and pairs well with Vercel.
- Built-in RLS lets us lock the tables down completely (server-only access).
- One store holds the hubs, the cached weather and FEMA data, score history, chat memory and the event log.
  No extra services.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet

A weather risk intelligence agent for a logistics company's US distribution hubs.
Analysts chat with it to find out which hubs are most exposed to severe weather, compare hubs,
and understand *why* a hub is risky, to help decide where to invest in resilience upgrades.

> 🚧 Work in progress. Built step by step. See [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md).

## Docs
- [Plan](docs/plan.md): architecture, tables, steps
- [Decision log](docs/decisions.md): every choice and why
- [Assumptions, uncertainty & scope](docs/assumptions.md)
- [Design](docs/design.md)
- [AI session log](docs/session/): the full conversation with the coding agent

## Run locally
Requirements: Node 22+, a Supabase project.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local     # then fill in the values (see comments in the file)
npm run db:check               # verifies the database connection: lists the hubs
npm run dev                    # http://localhost:3000
```

## Scripts
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` | Start the app locally |
| `npm test` | Unit tests (Vitest) |
| `npm run typecheck` | TypeScript check |
| `npm run lint` | ESLint (includes the rule keeping `src/core` free of Next.js) |
| `npm run db:check` | Connect to Supabase and list hubs per region |
| `npm run session:export -- <file.jsonl>` | Export the AI session log to `docs/session/` (scrubbed) |

## Database
SQL migrations live in [supabase/migrations/](supabase/migrations/). Apply them in order to a fresh
Supabase project (SQL editor or Supabase CLI). The second migration seeds the 36 hubs.

## Data attribution
Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Hazard data: FEMA National Risk Index.

# AI coding session log

The assignment asks for "the full session with the AI agent you worked with". This folder holds it.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `transcript.md` | The readable conversation: every message, every tool call and its result (long tool I/O truncated). |
| `transcript.jsonl` | The same conversation records, untruncated, in Claude Code's raw JSONL format. |

**How it was made:** `npm run session:export -- <session.jsonl>` (see [scripts/export-session.ts](../../scripts/export-session.ts)).

**What was removed:** email addresses, API keys and tokens, one-time login codes, the local home-folder
path, other people's usernames, and Claude Code's internal bookkeeping records. The model's private
reasoning blocks aren't included. The script fails if any of these items are still present after scrubbing.

**Where to start:** the planning ("grilling") rounds at the top of `transcript.md` show how every decision in
[../decisions.md](../decisions.md) was reached. Questions are numbered Q1–Q28.

Use this template for writing the PR body:

```markdown
## Summary

<diagram, diff-sketch, or tree>

## Evidence

- **Before:** <screenshot/output/failing test run>
  **After:** <screenshot/output/passing test run>

## Merge Danger

**Door:** <one-way or two-way>

<optional: description>

**Blast Radius:** <one-word description>

<optional: potential ramifications of merge>
```

## Sections

Skip all preambles and keep prose brief. Use the user's domain language from `GLOSSARY.md`.

### Summary

Pick the smallest view that makes the key point clear.

- Show logic or an algorithm as pseudocode:

```text
on(save)
  if content is unchanged
    return cached result
  write new content
  return fresh result
```

- Show runtime control flow as a call tree:

```text
submitForm
  createSession
    persistPrompt
    launchAgent
  navigateToSession
```

- Show UI structure as a component tree, including state and module boundaries that matter:

```text
<SessionPage> (apps/example/src/routes/session.tsx)
  useSessionEvents()
  <SessionToolbar>
    <RunSkillButton> (packages/ui)
```

- Show file responsibility or a broad refactor as a shallow file tree:

```text
src/
├── commands/       # parses user actions
├── sessions/       # owns session state
└── transport/      # sends API requests
```

- Show component interaction, control flow, or data flow with Mermaid:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant UI
    participant Daemon
    User->>UI: choose command
    UI->>Daemon: send expanded prompt
    Daemon-->>UI: stream result
```

- Use `diff` when the point is what changes and the surrounding shape already exists. Match the diff shape to the topic.

For a component change:

```diff
 <SessionPage>
   useSessionEvents()
   <SessionToolbar>
+    <RunSkillButton />
   <SessionTimeline>
+    <SkillResultCard />
```

For a file-layout change:

```diff
 src/
 ├── commands/
+│   └── show-me.ts       # expands the slash command
 ├── sessions/
-└── transport.ts
+└── transport/
+    ├── client.ts
+    └── stream.ts
```

For a call-tree or call-stack change:

```diff
 submitForm
   createSession
     persistPrompt
+    expandSkillMention
     launchAgent
-  navigateToSession
+  navigateToSession
+    subscribeToEvents
```

For a state or control-flow change:

```diff
 on(save)
-  write content
+  if content is unchanged
+    return cached result
+  write new content
+  invalidate cache
```

- Show the whole block when most of it is new, when omitted context would hide ownership or order, or when the user needs a copyable target shape:

```ts
function expandSkill(command: string): string {
  const skillName = command.slice(1);
  return `use the ${skillName} skill`;
}
```

#### Guidance

Place each visual next to the short text it supports. Keep only the calls, files, props, states, and boundaries needed to answer the user's current question or the options to resolve the current discussion point.

You may use one of these, you may use several, it is unlikely you will use all of them. Use your judgement and don't overwhelm the user.

### Evidence

Concrete evidence that the change works. Show a before and after.

Screenshots are S-tier - when the environment is set up for it and the change is visual.

Execution-based evidence is A-tier. Test results, console output. Show the exact test that now fails and passes, using pseudocode.

### Merge Danger

Describe whether it's a one-way or two-way door. You can walk back through two-way doors, but not one-way doors. A PR that is cheap to roll back is lower risk. Changes that involve destructive actions or hard-to-reverse decisions are one-way doors.

The blast radius is the potential impact or scope of the changes introduced by this PR. Consider all possibilities. Examples are layout shift, breakages for consumers, mobile responsiveness, etc.

input.content:
## Summary

Step 1 of [the plan](docs/plan.md): the foundation that later steps build on. The database is live, the hubs are seeded, the core folder is framework-free, the error format and env validation are in place, and the docs are started. No weather data or agent yet.

```text
src/
├── app/                  # Next.js only — placeholder page (Roboto, dark glass)
└── core/                 # framework-free (ESLint blocks next/react/app imports)
    ├── config/env.ts     # Zod-validated env, per-feature getters, never prints values
    ├── errors/           # "ErrorName || message || function || 🐘" + fixed emoji per boundary
    ├── domain/hub.ts     # Hub schema + US Census regions
    └── db/               # typed Supabase client, hubsRepository, eventsRepository
scripts/
├── check-db.ts           # npm run db:check
└── export-session.ts     # npm run session:export (scrub + built-in leak check)
supabase/migrations/      # schema + 36-hub seed (already applied to the live project)
docs/                     # plan, decisions (D1–D41), assumptions, design draft, session/
```

### Database (Supabase `daily-prophet`, us-east-1)

```mermaid
erDiagram
    hubs ||--o{ weather_daily : "1 row per day"
    hubs ||--o| fema_nri : "county record"
    hubs ||--o{ score_snapshots : "1 per ingest run"
    chat_sessions ||--o{ chat_messages : contains
    hubs |o--o{ events : "optional link"
    chat_sessions |o--o{ events : "optional link"
```

- Every table has `created_at` + `updated_at` (a shared trigger keeps `updated_at` current).
- `events` is an append-only log grouped by `correlation_id`. It replaces a separate `ingest_runs` table.
- RLS is on everywhere with **no policies**, so only the server's secret key can read or write.
- `score_snapshots.scoring_version` keeps "we changed the formula" from looking like "the weather changed".

## Decisions made in this step

The full log is in [docs/decisions.md](docs/decisions.md). The ones that land in code here:

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D31 | One Next.js app with `src/core/` free of Next.js, **enforced by ESLint** | Core logic stays testable and runnable from scripts and evals. Simpler than a monorepo |
| D33 | RLS on, no policies | Nothing is exposed even if the public key leaks |
| D34 | `created_at`/`updated_at` everywhere + `events` table | Track and analyze everything (your standing rule) |
| D35 | Boundary errors `Name \|\| message \|\| fn \|\| emoji`, fixed emoji per boundary (🦉 LLM, 🐸 Open-Meteo, 🦡 FEMA, 🐘 DB, 🦄 API, 🐍 Jev, 🦔 config) | Easy to locate. A fixed emoji is greppable |
| D36 | Readable hub IDs (`kansas-city`) | Clearer for the LLM, logs and humans |
| D37 | Tailwind (ships with the starter) | Fast glass UI, no extra dependency |
| D38 | Hub seed as a SQL migration, applied and committed | DB can be rebuilt from the repo |
| D39 | `@types/node` → v22 | Vitest 5 requires it, and it matches Node 22 |
| D40 | Single `.gitignore`-only commit pushed to `main` | An empty repo needs a base for PRs. Everything else goes through PRs |
| D41 | Session log exported with private details scrubbed + a leak check that fails the export | The repo is public |

**Things I noticed while setting up:**
- `create-next-app` refuses capital letters in the package name, so the package is named `daily-prophet`.
- Next 16 ships an `AGENTS.md` that `next dev` re-adds automatically, so it's committed.
- `.gitignore` had `.env*`, which would also have ignored `.env.example`. Added `!.env.example`.
- Added `.gitattributes` (LF line endings) to avoid CRLF churn on Windows.

## Evidence

```text
npm test        → Test Files 5 passed (5) · Tests 15 passed (15)
npm run typecheck → clean
npm run lint      → clean (incl. src/core boundary rule)
npm run build     → ✓ compiled, / prerendered
Supabase advisors → only "RLS enabled, no policy" (INFO) on our 7 tables — intended
session:export    → 🔒 Leak check passed: no emails, secrets, scrub terms or home path left
```

Tests cover:
- the error format
- env validation never leaking values
- hub row mapping, including rejecting unknown regions
- session scrubbing: emails removed but `zod@4.6.7` kept, tokens, every spelling of the home path
- transcript rendering skips reasoning blocks

⏳ **Still pending:** `npm run db:check`. It needs `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` in `.env.local`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

Code and docs can be reverted freely. The migrations are already applied to the live Supabase project, independent of this merge. They only *create* tables and insert seed rows, with nothing destructive.

**Blast Radius:** none

New project, no consumers yet.

## Env vars for this step

| Variable | Where |
|---|---|
| `SUPABASE_URL` | already in `.env.local` |
| `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` | Supabase → Project Settings → API Keys → Secret keys → paste into `.env.local` |

**What's in it:**

  - Every table has `created_at` / `updated_at`, kept current automatically by the database.
  - There's an `events` table that logs everything that happens. It replaces the separate ingest-runs table I'd planned.

- Supabase couldn't pause `my-trading-journal` through its API, so you paused it by hand.
- npm doesn't allow capital letters in package names, so the package is called `daily-prophet`.
- An empty repo needs one commit on `main` before a PR can target it. I pushed a single commit containing only `.gitignore`; everything else is in the PR.

3. **Review and merge PR #1** when you're happy.

**Next, Step 2:** fetch the weather and FEMA data and load it into the database. The first full download runs on your machine, paced to stay within Open-Meteo's limits, and takes roughly 1–2 hours. After that I'll check the real wind-gust numbers before we lock the 72 km/h tier. Step 2 needs no new `.env` values.

# Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → newest | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. Newest days lag about 5 days and are revised. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | Added because modeled gusts run low. Confirmed in Step 2 |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet

A weather risk intelligence agent for a logistics company's US distribution hubs.
Analysts chat with it to find out which hubs are most exposed to severe weather, compare hubs,
and understand *why* a hub is risky, to help decide where to invest in resilience upgrades.

> 🚧 Work in progress. Built step by step. See [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md).

## Docs
- [Plan](docs/plan.md): architecture, tables, steps
- [Decision log](docs/decisions.md): every choice and why
- [Assumptions, uncertainty & scope](docs/assumptions.md)
- [Design](docs/design.md)
- [AI session log](docs/session/): the full conversation with the coding agent

## Run locally
Requirements: Node 22+, a Supabase project.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local     # then fill in the values (see comments in the file)
npm run db:check               # verifies the database connection: lists the hubs
npm run dev                    # http://localhost:3000
```

## Scripts
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` | Start the app locally |
| `npm test` | Unit tests (Vitest) |
| `npm run typecheck` | TypeScript check |
| `npm run lint` | ESLint (includes the rule keeping `src/core` free of Next.js) |
| `npm run db:check` | Connect to Supabase and list hubs per region |
| `npm run session:export -- <file.jsonl>` | Export the AI session log to `docs/session/` (scrubbed) |

## Database
SQL migrations live in [supabase/migrations/](supabase/migrations/). Apply them in order to a fresh
Supabase project (SQL editor or Supabase CLI). The second migration seeds the 36 hubs.

## Data attribution
Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Hazard data: FEMA National Risk Index.

Step 2's code is written and tested (50 unit tests, type check and lint all clean). The full data download is now running in the background, and the PR isn't open yet. It started by accident: I meant to test one hub first, but PowerShell dropped the `--hub=denver` filter. Since the full download is this step's job anyway and is working correctly, I let it continue. The filter bug is fixed.

**How the download works:**
- **FEMA:** one call per hub, only for hubs that don't have a record yet.
- **Weather:** each hub gets its missing days plus the last 7 days again, because Open-Meteo revises its newest values. A new hub has 2021-01-01 to yesterday (2,154 days) to fill.
- **Rate limits:** a limiter counts Open-Meteo's weighted calls per minute, hour and day and pauses before hitting a limit. Failed requests are retried with a wait in between.
- **Failures:** if one hub fails, the rest carry on, and every step is written to the `events` table under one run ID.
- **Wrong data is rejected:** if Open-Meteo ever changes units (say, snowfall in inches) or FEMA fields go missing, the download fails instead of storing bad numbers.

**What we've learned so far:**
- **Open-Meteo has data up to yesterday**, not the 5-day lag I'd assumed. I've corrected the decision log and assumptions.
- **The first 13 hubs are complete:** 2,154 days each with no gaps, and the right counties (Cook for Chicago, Harris for Houston, Fulton for Atlanta).
- **FEMA leaves hazards blank where they don't apply,** e.g. Denver has no hurricane value and Miami has no ice-storm value.

**When the download finishes (about 1 hour total, because of Open-Meteo's hourly limit):**
1. Check that all 36 hubs are complete.
2. **Check wind gusts:** count how many days per year each hub has gusts ≥ 93 km/h vs ≥ 72 km/h, to settle whether we need the second tier.
3. Run a second ingest to prove it's incremental: it should fetch only 7 days per hub.
4. Open **PR #2** with those results.

While we wait, two quick things from you:
1. **The session log** in [docs/session/transcript.md](docs/session/transcript.md): is the cleaned version OK to publish? I won't push it until you say so.
2. If you have time, **create your OpenRouter key** (with the $20 cap). Step 4 will need it as `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in `.env.local`.
its ok. i noticed you were using fetch for the https config, why not axios? any specific reason?

Thanks. I'll take "it's ok" as approval of the cleaned session log, and include it in PR #2 unless you tell me otherwise.

**Why `fetch` and not axios:** no strong reason against axios. `fetch` was simply the better fit here:

1. **It's built in.** Node 22 and Vercel's runtime both have `fetch`, so there's one dependency fewer to install, update and audit.
2. **Axios's main advantages don't help us much.** Axios throws on 4xx/5xx and parses JSON for you, but that's about 3 lines in our wrapper. Axios also **doesn't retry on its own** (you'd add `axios-retry`), and we needed custom rules anyway: retry 429/5xx and network errors, honor `Retry-After`, and use our error format. So the wrapper in [http.ts](src/core/data/http.ts) is about 60 lines either way.
3. **Timeouts are built in:** `AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)` is standard and needs no extra setup.
4. **Tests are simple.** The wrapper takes any fetch-like function, so tests pass in a fake that returns a real `Response` object. No mocking library needed.
5. **It matches the rest of the stack.** The Vercel AI SDK, the OpenRouter provider and supabase-js all use `fetch` internally, so the whole app makes HTTP calls the same way.

**When I'd pick axios:** if we needed interceptors across many APIs (shared auth headers, request logging), upload/download progress, or support for old Node versions. We need none of these, and our wrapper is the one shared "interceptor" layer.

My recommendation is to keep `fetch`. Swapping later would be cheap, because only [http.ts](src/core/data/http.ts) calls it directly. If you'd still prefer axios, say so and I'll switch.

I'll add this to the decision log:

# Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → yesterday, in each hub's local calendar day | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. The last few days are **preliminary** and get revised, so we re-fetch the last 7 every night. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | Added because modeled gusts run low. Confirmed in Step 2 |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

content.text: Since we're waiting anyway, I'll run the wind-gust check on the 29 hubs already loaded. That's the open question from Q28: do days with gusts ≥ 93 km/h show up at all in this modeled data?

input.query:
with w as (
  select hub_id, wind_gust_max_kmh g from weather_daily
  where date > (current_date - interval '5 years') and date < current_date
)
select hub_id,
  round(count(*) filter (where g >= 93) / 5.0, 1) as warn_days_per_yr,
  round(count(*) filter (where g >= 72) / 5.0, 1) as advisory_days_per_yr,
  round(count(*) filter (where g >= 60) / 5.0, 1) as ge60_per_yr,
  max(g) as max_gust,
  round(percentile_cont(0.99) within group (order by g)::numeric, 1) as p99
from w group by hub_id order by advisory_days_per_yr desc;

  round(count(*) filter (where g >= 60) / 5.0, 1) as ge60_per_yr,
  max(g) as max_gust,
  round(percentile_cont(0.99) within group (order by g)::numeric, 1) as p99
from w group by hub_id order by advisory_days_per_yr desc;

**What it means:**
- **Warning-level gust days barely appear in this data.** 11 of 29 hubs show zero in 5 years, though real windstorms clearly happened. As expected, the modeled data smooths out peaks.

# Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → yesterday, in each hub's local calendar day | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. The last few days are **preliminary** and get revised, so we re-fetch the last 7 every night. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |

Error Handling - we already talked about it but it would be nice to have that in the rules file for the project.

Always wrap operations in try/catch blocks. Error messages must follow this format:

`ErrorName || message || functionName || emoji`

JSDoc

Always add JSDoc comments to every function, class, method, and type you write and explain clearly and simply as possible.

Before Writing Code

1. Check for existing implementations - Before creating any new function, utility, type, or component, search the codebase for something that already does the same thing. Reuse over reinvent.
2. Check for usages - Before modifying or creating something, check if it's used elsewhere in the codebase. Flag any side effects or mention impacted areas.

Vibes

 External Calls (critical)

When planning anything, minimize risk surface and protect a single source of truth:

- Fewer risky steps wins. Prefer the plan with the smallest number of moving parts that can fail (network calls, manual steps, multi-step migrations, parallel writes). If two plans reach the same outcome, pick the one with fewer ways to break.
- One source of truth, always. Never let the same fact live in two places that can drift. If a value is derivable, derive it — don't cache a copy unless cache invalidation is explicitly designed. When you spot duplication of state, config, or schema, flag it before coding.

Anti-Hallucination

Before you (Claude) claim something exists, a file, function, table, column, env var, package, endpoint, command, flag, verify it. Read the file, grep the symbol, check the schema, run `--help`. Stating "X exists" without checking is a hallucination risk, even when it feels obvious. If you're not sure, say so explicitly instead of guessing, surfaced uncertainty is always better than a confident wrong answer.

Hard-Won Lessons

Before I write anything, here's my honest read. Most of these rules are good. A few conflict with what we already agreed, one exposes a gap in my own code, and one section is empty. Since we decide together, here's a round of questions, each with my recommendation. Answering "yes" accepts it.

---

❓ **R1** - **"Always wrap operations in try/catch" contradicts our earlier rule.** In Step 1 we agreed: *catch at the boundaries* (external APIs, database, LLM, Jev, API routes), and *pure functions just throw*. Taken literally, "always" leads to:

- longer messages that are harder to read,
- error formats that differ depending on which layer caught them.

Proposed wording: *"Wrap every boundary operation (external call, DB, LLM, Jev, API route, script entry point) in try/catch and rethrow in the `ErrorName || message || functionName || emoji` format. Pure functions throw plain errors and let the boundary format them. Never swallow an error silently. If you deliberately continue (like `recordEvent`), log it in the format."*

| Fact | Lives in | Risk | Proposed fix |
|---|---|---|---|

| Event sources (`ingest`, `agent`, …) | DB check constraint **and** TS `EventSource` type | Real drift risk | A test that reads the live constraint and compares it to the TS list |

6. **Switching to an older `main` after a merge leaves "untracked files would be overwritten"** → compare file hashes before any reset. Nothing was actually lost.
